description: We are BORAMAE, a team of two serving in the Republic of Korea Air Force. Chanhui Lee develops software for the Intelligent Information Systems Management Group under ROKAF HQ, while Jaewon Choi manages space weather data in the Space Operations Group under ROKAF Operations Command. For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to combine our expertise to build a web app that turns a question about a place into a statistically tested NASA data trend, with every number traceable to its source.
summary:
BORAMAE is a bilingual (English/Korean) web app that turns a plain question about a place, such as "Is Seoul's first snow coming later?", into a statistically tested NASA trend.

An AI parser proposes NASA variables with one-line definitions; the user confirms them, pins an area and sets a time window. The app then builds an area-averaged series from NASA POWER (MERRA-2) data since 1981 and tests it with a Theil–Sen slope and 95% confidence interval, an autocorrelation-corrected Mann–Kendall test and an OLS t-test, giving a plain-language verdict. 

This covers all four challenge objectives: identifying variables, acquiring them for a region, visualizing a long time series and testing its rate of change. When a trend is significant, a "case board" tests the processes driving it and responding to it on the same data; otherwise the app points to other variables, nearby regions or the record length still needed.

It matters because NASA's tools stop at the chart, while students rarely know which variable to pick or what "significant" means. Every number traces to its dataset and method, and AI never produces one.
details:
Ask NASA data a question about your place, and get an honest, tested answer.

BORAMAE is a bilingual English-Korean web app. It turns a question such as "Is Seoul's first snow coming later?" into a NASA time series for a pinned area and tests it for a trend. When the trend is significant, it then tests the processes that drive and respond to the change, on the same data.

Try it: Phoenix, 110 °F days (English): https://d3gct1libr2d5x.cloudfront.net/en/?demo=hot-days-phoenix&at=result · Seoul, first snow (Korean): https://d3gct1libr2d5x.cloudfront.net/ko/?demo=first-snow-seoul&at=result

1. The problem we defined

NASA already holds the data for everyday climate questions. The two NASA POWER stores we read carry 74 daily and 472 monthly variables. Turning a question into a defensible answer still takes expert steps: picking the right variable and area, removing the seasonal cycle, and testing the trend without being fooled when one year resembles the next. NASA's tools mostly stop at the chart. Giovanni plots more than 2,000 variables, but its optional regression line is not a trend verdict. Worldview's charting tool, still in beta, gives summary statistics such as the mean and median, but no trend test. Students, the challenge's audience, rarely know how long a record must be or what "significant" means.

Hypothesis: a first-time student can reach a tested, explained trend in about two minutes if one tool does three things. It picks the right NASA yearly metric. It tests that metric with calibrated statistics that can say "not yet." And it tests the linked processes on the same data instead of narrating them.

2. What BORAMAE does

Three doors lead to the same tested result: Start investigating, Explore freely (click any point on the map for a quick trend card) and Watch a demo (two scripted, captioned cases in the real interface).

The guided path has four steps. Each step has a Back button and a "Skip to explore" button.

  1. Ask in English or Korean, or tap one of six example questions, picked from a set of 23 for the country in view and the season.
  2. Confirm. BORAMAE proposes up to three NASA variables, each with a plain definition. For a typed question, each one also shows why it was picked. The app reads the investigation back in one sentence, and nothing runs until you confirm.
  3. Pin the place with a 10–300 km radius. The grid cells to be averaged appear before the run.
  4. Set the years, from 1981 to the latest published month. Under 20 years, the verdict is withheld.

The case panel then shows:

  • Chart, then verdict. The chart shows the yearly series and first asks "Does this look like a trend?" so the student commits to a guess. The card then gives the rate per decade with its confidence interval, the Mann–Kendall p-value and an OLS cross-check. It states the result in plain words: significant rise or fall, not yet significant, no trend detected or record too short.
  • If significant: the case board. The app tests up to three drivers and three responses on the same data and years. Each arrow shows its result, its cited source and a label: consistent, weak, contradicts or not testable here. Contradictions stay on the board.
  • If not: the no-trend fallback. It lists other variables that do trend in the same area, found by a scan with false-discovery-rate control. Inside East Asia, it also searches a precomputed first-snow trend grid for the nearest areas within 1,000 km where the trend is significant, and marks them "same process, opposite directions" when the sign flips. In the Seoul demo, no nearby area passes the correction. The fallback also says how many more years the current rate needs.
  • Provenance for every number on the verdict card and the case board: dataset ID and version, access path, cells, period, method, where the number was computed and how much data the query reads.

Image: case board en hot-days phoenix

Image: Seoul, first snow trend analysis

3. How it works

NASA data. Every verdict runs on NASA POWER. POWER serves daily and monthly surface fields from MERRA-2, NASA's reanalysis, from 1981 on a ½° × ⅝° grid. A reanalysis is a weather model that assimilates satellite and ground observations into one consistent record. POWER sits as anonymous Zarr arrays in the AWS Open Data bucket nasa-power, so any land point gets 45 years of data with no login. We curated 20 variables, from temperature and snowfall to soil wetness, sea ice and ozone.

Question to yearly metric. The question becomes a spec whose variables and metrics must be catalog IDs. Units follow the place, so "110-degree days" in Phoenix reads as 110 °F (43.3 °C). The service averages the grid cells inside the area, weighted by cell area. It then reduces the series to one value per year, so the test answers the question that was asked. That value can be a seasonal mean, total or maximum (such as the wettest day), a first date, a count of days past a threshold, the length of the frost-free season, a season's onset or length (KMA's 9-day running-mean rule), or degree-days. First snow, for example, is the first day with at least 0.1 mm of snow water after 1 August. A year with no snow is kept as censored, not dropped.

Trend test. Each yearly series gets three tests:

  • a Theil–Sen slope with a 95% confidence interval, per decade in the metric's own units (Sen 1968);
  • Mann–Kendall with a lag-1 correction for serial correlation after Hamed & Rao (1998), always applied and never allowed to shrink the variance;
  • an OLS slope with an AR(1)-adjusted sample size, as a cross-check (Santer et al. 2000).

A trend is significant only when the Mann–Kendall p is below 0.05 and the Sen interval excludes zero. "Not yet" and "no trend" cards estimate the years still needed, after Weatherhead et al. (1998), adapted to yearly values. Every scanned list is controlled with Benjamini–Hochberg at q = 0.10.

Case board test. Two trending series always correlate, so a shared trend proves nothing. Instead, each arrow is tested on how the two series move together from year to year. The app detrends both series, pairs them at the lag the literature gives and correlates them with an effective-sample-size correction (α = 0.05, at least 10 overlapping years). The sign must match the expected one. The board says "consistent with," never "caused by." Every link comes from a cited registry, with a DOI or URL, the scale at which the link holds and its status: robust, contested, weak or not testable here.

Checked against NASA's own tools. We started from the challenge's worked example, the SeaWiFS chlorophyll study (Acker et al. 2009), which box-averaged satellite data in Giovanni and fitted regression lines. Its box-average-then-regress workflow survives in BORAMAE as the OLS cross-check, but our verdicts rest on tests that paper did not apply: Mann–Kendall with a lag-1 Hamed–Rao correction, a Theil–Sen confidence interval and a 20-year minimum record. We then rebuilt the Phoenix demo in NASA Giovanni from MERRA-2 daily maximum temperature (M2SDNXSLV T2MMAX) over the same grid cell. Giovanni gives the same verdict: a significant rise of 3.4 days per decade (95% CI 1.4 to 5.6, p = 0.002), against BORAMAE's 3.3 (1.4 to 5.0, p = 0.002). Its yearly counts match ours in 11 of 45 years and are never lower, at most 6 days higher (r = 0.99), because its daily maximum runs 0.22 °C warmer on average.

Architecture. The browser loads a static Next.js app and receives only results. A FastAPI service on Amazon ECS runs in us-west-2, next to the POWER bucket. It reads only the Zarr chunks it needs and runs every statistic. Each result is stored once in Amazon S3 as an unchangeable JSON file, named by a hash of the spec, the dataset version and the engine version. Identical questions therefore share one file, and a rerun gives the same bytes. Amazon CloudFront and AWS WAF serve the app and the API on one domain. Batch jobs precompute the demo cases and a 4,941-cell first-snow trend grid over East Asia for the nearby-area search. The demos ship inside the static site, so a local copy plays them with the network off.

Image: boramae aws architecture diagram; ai generated

AI, with guardrails. AI never computes a result. A model on Amazon Bedrock only proposes the investigation spec: the catalog variable IDs, the place, the months and the threshold. You see the proposal, the pin and the grid cells, and nothing runs until you confirm. Every statistic comes from the engine. A Korean–English keyword parser (첫눈 → snowfall, 폭염 → hot days) takes over whenever the model is off or fails, so the app works fully without the LLM. (Details in Use of SI.)

4. Why we designed it this way

  • Most of our effort went past the verdict. Mann–Kendall and Sen's slope on a map are now a common entry for this challenge. So we put our work into what follows the verdict: testing the processes behind a change, as the challenge asks.
  • The tool recommends, and the student decides. Every suggestion shows its basis, and nothing runs unconfirmed.
  • Honest outcomes are first-class. "Not yet" and "no trend" each lead to a next step.
  • English-first, not English-only. Every interface string exists in both languages, and one heat board serves both "33 °C days in Daegu" and "110 °F days in Phoenix."
  • Compute beside the data. Reading POWER in its own AWS Region keeps analyses fast and lets each result report how much data it moved.

5. What we tested, and how NASA data changed our design

  • An off-the-shelf correction over-called trends. In a pre-event check of 2,000 trend-free series per setting, pymannkendall's default Hamed–Rao option called 8–9% of white-noise series significant, and 12–13% at a lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.2, against a nominal 5%. So we wrote our own engine on NumPy and SciPy and kept the libraries as test references. Our lag-1 correction, applied every time, gave 4.3% and 7.3% in our published run (1,000 series of 45 years per setting, fixed seed). The 7.3% misses the 7% limit we set ourselves, and our Methods page reports it as a fail.
  • Twenty years is only a minimum. A pre-event simulation used a real warming of 0.3 °C per decade with 0.5 °C of year-to-year scatter and a lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.2. The corrected test found the trend in 8% of 10-year records, 26% of 20-year, 65% of 30-year and 94% of 40-year ones. Hence the record guard and the years-needed estimate.
  • Stored precision changed a count. POWER stores values as scaled integers. Decoded in single precision, a stored 0.10 mm reads as 0.09998 and fails a "≥ 0.1 mm" first-snow test. At the Seoul cell, 40 days since 1981 sit exactly at 0.10 mm, so 986 days meet the threshold, not 946. We confirmed the encoding on 4.7 million stored values. The reader now rounds each value to the decimals its variable declares.
  • Variable names can mislead. POWER's monthly T2M_MAX is the hottest hour of each month, not the mean of daily highs, so those metrics read the daily store. CDD18_3 already holds degree-days, so we sum it instead of computing degree-days from it again.
  • The data chose our demo story. We planned to open on a Seoul first-snow case board, but Seoul's first-snow date does not reach significance. That demo now shows the no-trend fallback, and the case board demo runs on Phoenix's 110 °F days, which do reach it.
  • Engineering checks. The Python and TypeScript encoders must reproduce the same eight golden test vectors, and both sides pass the same 13 cell-selection cases. Area averaging is checked against an independent reference within 0.1%. With the autocorrelation term off, our Sen-interval rule matched SciPy's theilslopes on 8,000 of 8,000 tie-free synthetic series. With the term on, as shipped, our interval is wider than SciPy's. A linter blocks any registry link that has no source.

6. Benefits and impact

  • Students go from their own question to a tested answer in minutes. Along the way they practice three habits: a trend needs a long record, "not significant" is not "no change," and "consistent with" is not "caused by."
  • Teachers get a ready class activity: captioned demos for Seoul and Phoenix that run offline, in English or Korean. Students' own cities run live in the same interface.
  • Anyone checking a news claim, such as "summers are getting longer," can test it on 45 years of NASA data. They can also see which data and method gave the answer.
  • New content needs no code. The trend test works at any land point. A new place is one gazetteer entry. A new case board is one board entry plus one cited registry row for each link.
  • Open and lasting. The project is Apache 2.0, needs no account and stores no personal data. It runs on AWS beside the data and stays online at least until the Global Winners announcement on January 27, 2027.

7. Limitations and next steps

  • Scale. MERRA-2 is a model constrained by observations, with grid cells about 50 km across. It cannot resolve a city's heat island: Phoenix's cell counts about 6.6 fewer 110 °F days a year than the Sky Harbor airport station (GHCN-Daily, 1981–2025), but the two trends agree (+3.3 and +3.9 days per decade) and the yearly counts correlate at r = 0.85. Our first-snow date is a threshold on model snowfall, not KMA's observed first snow.
  • Cause. The case board shows consistency with known mechanisms, not proof of cause. Four boards ship today: snow, heat, heavy rain and seasons. Fourteen more are designed, from drought and wildfire to Arctic sea ice.
  • Persistence. Some series change slowly from year to year, with a lag-1 autocorrelation near 0.4, as groundwater and sea-surface temperature do. For those, even the corrected test gives false alarms about 10% of the time (9.7% in our run). The Methods page shows this rate next to the others.
  • Next: a guide chat that can fly the map, set the area and years, and explain a result, with a badge on every AI sentence and our number guard (already built and tested) checking each one. Then an independent re-run of the Seoul demo in KNMI Climate Explorer, station overlays in the app (KMA ASOS, NOAA GHCN-Daily), finer NASA sources (GPM IMERG, GLDAS, and MODIS through AppEEARS), share links and a test with outside students.

8. Tools and technologies

  • Languages: TypeScript, Python
  • Data: NASA POWER (MERRA-2) for every verdict; NASA Giovanni (MERRA-2 M2SDNXSLV) and NOAA GHCN-Daily for independent checks; Natural Earth and Wikidata for the base map and place names
  • Frontend: Next.js (static export), React, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, TanStack Query, MapLibre GL JS, D3, next-intl (English and Korean), Pretendard font
  • Analysis service: FastAPI, pydantic, xarray, zarr, fsspec, NumPy, SciPy; pymannkendall and statsmodels as test references
  • AI: Amazon Bedrock (Converse API) for the question parser
  • Cloud (Amazon AWS): Amazon S3, Amazon CloudFront, AWS WAF, Amazon ECS Express Mode (AWS Fargate, Arm), Amazon CloudWatch, Application Load Balancer
  • Testing: pytest, Vitest, Testing Library, and a linter for the hand-written content files
  • Hardware: our own laptops
  • AI assistance in development: see Use of SI

9. Use of Super Intelligence

We used AI at every stage, and our team reviewed all of its output. AI assistants helped us research NASA data sources and check our trend methods. Every number in the app comes from Python statistics code, not from a language model. A number guard withholds any AI sentence with a number missing from the analysis data, and a badge marks each AI sentence. Claude Code wrote and debugged our code and tests. AI also helped us draft and edit our English and Korean text, interface design, and demo slides.
